evidence_set: Registered review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224): 22 studies (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) out of 73 candidate articles; 3 rated high risk of bias. Five databases, 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018, English only; people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use (no restriction by route is stated). 13 distinct outcomes, 5 poolable. The review frames its exposure as marijuana use, says smoking remains the main method of consumption and words its conclusion for smoking marijuana, but does not say every study was of smoking; use was quantified in joints and joint-years among other ways (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).

Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against nonusers (the Methods define nonusers as people using neither cannabis nor tobacco; the Results call them nonsmokers): cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms. The abstract and Results report the pooled intervals (which exclude 1) as showing an increased risk; the Figure 2 legend gives the Knapp-Hartung P values.

Cross-sectional studies pooled (the Abstract gives 1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias; the Table gives 4 studies, 1 low and 3 moderate, for the wheezing pool and does not give the number pooled for the other outcomes; all studies included moderate to heavy use), people who used cannabis against nonusers (the Methods define nonusers as people using neither cannabis nor tobacco; the Results call them nonsmokers): cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum production RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13). Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01. Heterogeneity was high for wheezing; the Discussion says heterogeneity limited the cough, sputum and wheezing analyses and was likely related to non-uniform assessment of cannabis use and of outcomes (for example, cough definitions). For dyspnea the ratio's interval excludes 1 while the difference's includes 0. Which studies were pooled is shown only in a forest-plot image (Figure 3), which was not read.

Chronic bronchitis and COPD: the Los Angeles cohort (3.0 joints a day, mean 9.8 years, 49% lost) found an increased risk of bronchitis episodes compared with nonuse, OR 2.3 (1.2 to 4.4), P = 0.011. Three cross-sectional studies pooled: RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16), not significant (Knapp-Hartung P = 0.31). SPIROMICS (n = 1174, a sample of only people currently or formerly smoking tobacco): current use OR 0.87 (0.59 to 1.31), former use OR 1.0 (0.79 to 1.26). A high-risk-of-bias study found COPD prevalence higher by 0.3% (0.0% to 0.5%) per joint-year, with people who used cannabis and tobacco combined.

FEV1: CARDIA (rated low risk of bias; 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start): current use, adjusted mean difference −18 mL (−42 to 6.1) against nonsmokers (the review's word); a Los Angeles cohort (mean age 33, over 3.5 joints a day, 8 years): no significant fall in people who smoked cannabis continuously or intermittently against people who did not smoke it; Dunedin (10 years): no change. FVC: CARDIA lifetime use over 10 joint-years +59 mL (12 to 107); cross-sectional SPIROMICS higher FVC in current and former use and NHANES +0.07% per joint-year (NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking combined). The review describes the CARDIA −18 mL as minimal exposure and attaches trend P values (0.32, 0.03, 0.01) to single contrasts; in the primary paper the −18 mL contrast is the heaviest current category and those P values are for trend, so CARDIA is cited from the primary paper (anchors below).

Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week, moderate risk of bias): significant FEV1 reductions after 1 year (P < 0.01) and a significant reduction in the FEV1-FVC ratio. NHANES 2007 to 2010 (low risk of bias): more than 20 joint-years against people who did not smoke cannabis, ratio below 70%, OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9) after tobacco adjustment (the earlier NHANES study, moderate risk of bias: no definite relationship); SPIROMICS (mean 30.1 joint-years, all with a tobacco-smoking history): current smoking positively associated with the FEV1-FVC ratio, P < 0.001 (the review's wording; read literally a higher ratio, so the direction is unclear); a Wellington study (n = 339, mean 54.2 joint-years) marginally lower ratio, −1.1% (−2.6% to 0.1%). All four studies of airway resistance and specific conductance (1 prospective, low risk of bias; 3 cross-sectional) found higher resistance and lower conductance in people who smoked cannabis.

One model with all four smoking variables (current and lifetime cannabis and tobacco). Cannabis, four-level categories, tobacco in the same model: lifetime exposure was associated with higher FVC and FEV1 than zero exposure (1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL, 15 to 62; FVC +41 mL, 14 to 67; 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL, 32 to 100; FVC +54 mL, 16 to 91; over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL, -6.5 to 79; FVC +59 mL, 12 to 107). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) was FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) and FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49) against no current use. In a separate model of current smoking status, without the other three variables, people who used cannabis only differed little from people using neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, -12 to 13; FVC +8.2 mL, -5 to 22), while tobacco only was -24 mL (-38 to -11) for FEV1. The Results text gives the top lifetime category as 'more than 20' joint-years while Table 2 labels it 'more than 10'; Table 2's label is used.

Current intensity, spline models: non-linear for both outcomes (FEV1 P = 0.025, FVC P = 0.035). At 20 episodes a month the FEV1 slope was -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6, P = 0.017) and the FVC slope -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); net differences against no exposure at 20 episodes a month were FEV1 +14 mL (-4.7 to 32) and FVC +43 mL (23 to 63). No data at 40 episodes a month. The authors state the net FEV1 association became negative only at very high exposure (over 40 joint-years or 25 episodes a month) and not significantly.

Tobacco (positive control): current smoking of more than 20 cigarettes a day was associated with FEV1 63 mL lower than zero exposure (95% CI -89 to -36) and FVC 69 mL lower (-97 to -41); lifetime exposure over 20 pack-years with FEV1 101 mL lower than zero exposure (-136 to -65). In spline models the association was linear and dose-related, with a slope of -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years and net differences against no exposure at 50 pack-years of -332 mL (-401 to -263) for FEV1 and -229 mL (-310 to -147) for FVC. No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis exposure was found for FEV1 or FVC.

Respiratory outcome, cannabis users against controls within each tobacco-history group: people currently or formerly smoking tobacco OR 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04 (123 events, 3.5%, against 290, 4.2%); people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record OR 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70). All-cause outcome: 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26) and 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56). Within each sex, respiratory OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31) in men and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10) in women; within each pre-existing asthma or COPD group, respiratory OR 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11) with and 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20) without. One row of Table 4 is internally inconsistent (events in the cannabis group 149 + 33 = 182, not the 175 of Table 2); people with missing tobacco status are analysed with people who never smoked tobacco.

The authors accept that the null respiratory result may be real but give reasons it may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings. Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province. The Discussion's threshold of 20 joints per year for lung-function decline cites two papers (Tan 2019 and Pletcher 2012); it reads as a rate, whereas the CARDIA paper's measure is cumulative joint-years, and that paper did not establish a threshold at 20 joint-years (net FEV1 difference +27 mL, -10 to 64); the Tan paper was not read.

Respiratory symptoms (Conclusion 7-3): the committee graded as substantial the evidence of a statistical association (7-3a) between long-term cannabis smoking and worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent chronic bronchitis episodes, and as moderate the evidence of an association (7-3b) between stopping and improvement. Under it: a 2007 systematic review of 14 symptom studies (nine cross-sectional, three case series, one case-control, one cohort; cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0); the Wellington cross-sectional study (cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%, people who smoked cannabis against nonsmokers); the Dunedin cohort of 1,037 followed to age 38 (frequent use, defined as 52 or more times in the past year, against under 52 times, which the committee calls nonusers: morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; fewer symptoms after quitting); an internet survey of 5,987 adults recruited through drug-policy-reform organisations; a longitudinal cohort of 299 followed for at least two visits over 9.8 years, with high or variable loss to follow-up (current against never use: cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4; current against former use: cough 3.3, sputum 4.2, wheeze 2.1). The committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both cannabis and tobacco on symptoms.

Limits of the symptom evidence as the committee states them: most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking; many did not control for tobacco and occupational or environmental exposures, or for dose or duration; many did not use joint-years and instead based heavy exposure on exceeding a threshold of cigarettes, and even among studies that used joint-years the THC content of a joint is potentially highly variable between joints and between years; Dunedin classed fewer than 52 uses a year as non-use and did not know whether cannabis was smoked; the internet survey recruited through organisations advocating drug-policy reform.

Lung function (Conclusion 7-1): 'moderate evidence' of an association between cannabis smoking and improved airway dynamics with acute use but not chronic use (7-1a) and with higher FVC (7-1b); the chapter highlight says it is unclear whether cannabis use is associated with worsened lung function. Under it: the 2007 review (34 publications; acute bronchodilation; regular smoking associated with lower specific airway conductance, about 16% on average, and a lower FEV1; inconsistent findings otherwise); CARDIA, 5,115 adults over 20 years, occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with adverse effects on lung function, with a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure (20 or more joint-years) and with few people at heavy exposure; Dunedin (1,037, spirometry at 32): cumulative cannabis associated with higher FVC, total lung capacity and residual volume but not lower FEV1 or FEV1/FVC; NHANES 2007 to 2012 (10,327 adults, cross-sectional): lower FEV1/FVC and higher FEV1 and FVC in people who had smoked cannabis recently than in never smokers of cannabis; a 12-person vaporizer feasibility study with no control group.

Wellington sample (Aldington et al., 2007; convenience sample of 339; entry required at least 5 joint-years of cannabis or 1 pack-year of tobacco, according to what was smoked; self-reported use): no association between long-term cannabis smoking and the lung-function variables, but when analysed per joint-year a significantly lower FEV1/FVC, lower specific airways conductance and higher total lung capacity than in nonsmokers; the authors estimated that each joint's association with a lower FEV1/FVC was similar to that of 2.5 to 5 tobacco cigarettes. The committee criticises the analysis: only main effects were reported (no test of interaction between cannabis and tobacco) and coefficients were labelled odds ratios in two tables. The committee cites the same paper for the symptom percentages.

COPD (Conclusion 7-2): 'limited evidence' of an association between occasional cannabis smoking and developing COPD when controlled for tobacco use (7-2a); 'insufficient evidence' for hospital admissions for COPD (7-2b). Under it: Wellington CT scans (the same paper as the 339-person sample; the number scanned is not given) with inconsistent results; Vancouver cross-sectional study of 878 adults (at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco history: not at significantly greater risk of COPD or more respiratory symptoms; tobacco plus cannabis not clearly different from tobacco only); a 709-person readmission study (cannabis 0.22 against tobacco 0.26, unit not specified); a 500-person cross-sectional study with no non-smoking group (COPD 24.3% tobacco only against 25.2% tobacco plus cannabis, p = 0.90; more cough, phlegm and wheeze with both, no adjusted comparison); NHANES (more than 20 joint-years against no cannabis exposure, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.9, but higher FVC and no FEV1 association, and pre-bronchodilator spirometry). The Discussion says it is unclear whether regular use is associated with developing or worsening COPD and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally once tobacco is controlled for. The basis for the word occasional in Conclusion 7-2(a) is not apparent in the text read: the studies described do not show an association in people who smoke cannabis occasionally.

Background given for smoke exposure: data from 15 volunteers suggest that smoking one cannabis joint can lead to four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times more tar deposition than smoking a single cigarette; the committee says this may be, in part, because people who smoke cannabis generally inhale more deeply and hold their breath longer than people who smoke cigarettes and because cannabis cigarettes do not commonly have filters. Against this, cannabis cigarettes are not as densely packed and people who use cannabis usually smoke fewer of them per day than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes.

Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The committee says its hierarchy of evidence does not imply how large the observed effect is or how much the health effect matters to individuals or populations, and that its terms reflect the quality, quantity and consistency of the evidence. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied). The Chapter 7 highlight predicts that stopping will probably reduce chronic cough and phlegm, causal wording over Conclusion 7-3(b), which grades only an association; of the studies cited for cessation, only the Tashkin et al. (2012) cohort of 299 participants is noted for high rates of loss to follow-up or variable follow-up periods. Appendix B does not place cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7, in its order of evidence.

Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, Subramaniam et al., 2016); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

evidence_set: Epidemiologic review (Huang et al., 2015; no meta-analysis) of six lung cancer studies, including the pooled analysis and two of its studies. Of the three others, two were described by the pooled analysis's authors as having several limitations, among them inadequate control of tobacco use and potential reporting bias, and the committee does not discuss them; the third, a cohort of 49,321 Swedish male military conscripts followed 40 years (44,257 in the cannabis analysis; Callaghan et al., 2013), found a hazard ratio of 2.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 4.14) for those who reported using cannabis more than 50 times at baseline against those who reported never using it, adjusted for tobacco and alcohol use and other confounders (the footnote lists tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription). The committee says the studies in the review but not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk. No absolute risks are given. The cohort paper itself was not read.

The committee's graded conclusion 5-1 (quoted here) is its judgment. The chapter does not say what the grade rests on: the Discussion reports that the pooled analysis found no significant association, that studies in the review but not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk, and the limits of the Swedish cohort. Box B-3 defines moderate as several supportive findings from studies of good to fair quality, with very few or no credible opposing findings, where chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence. The Chapter 5 highlight goes further than the numbered conclusion (it says the evidence suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk of lung and head and neck cancer in adults), and the Chapter 5 Summary words the conclusion as no statistically significant association between cannabis use (not specifically smoking) and lung or head and neck cancer. Reader's comment, not the committee's: the grade reads wider than the pooled interval allows, since the interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the cohort hazard ratio is 2.12, and the Box B-3 definition asks for very few or no credible opposing findings; the chapter does not explain how these were weighed.

Chapter 5 gaps and summary: the committee judged the evidence on lung and head and neck cancer moderate for no statistically significant association; it lists small samples, low participation, unverifiable self-reported use and difficulty controlling confounders as challenges similar to those in studies of other clinical outcomes; it adds challenges special, if not unique, to cancer studies: risk factors such as family cancer history, occupational exposures and diet are hard to measure and were often not accounted for, and the long incubation of many cancers requires a similarly long observation period; and it asks for studies that confirm the existing evidence on lung and head and neck cancers and for replication, because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies.

Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4; the Search 6 listing names only Embase and Medline) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), first sorted into seven major health endpoint topic areas and later divided into the 11 topic areas of the report's chapters; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999. Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then assessed on five attributes adapted from other sources (Higgins et al., 2011) and rated good, fair or poor, each independently by at least two members (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed. Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The committee says its hierarchy of evidence does not imply how large the observed effect is or how much the health effect matters to individuals or populations, and that its terms reflect the quality, quantity and consistency of the evidence. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several supportive findings from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied).

Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, Subramaniam et al., 2016); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

Table 1 sets the report's conclusions beside the WHO report's. Respiratory rows: bronchitis and respiratory symptoms (substantial evidence for increased incidence and symptom severity in long-term cannabis users; moderate for improvement after cessation of use), pulmonary function (moderate for acute but not chronic use causing bronchodilatation; moderate for higher lung volume, which the table prints as long volume, but clinical significance is unclear and control for tobacco smoking effects was poor), COPD (limited evidence for increased risk in occasional cannabis smokers, controlled for tobacco smoking; insufficient for COPD severity), asthma (no or insufficient). Cancer rows: lung and head and neck cancers moderate evidence for no association, against WHO's statement that a smoking mix of cannabis and tobacco may increase cancer risks and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown. Table 1 words the committee's cancer conclusion without the word statistical; the WHO report was not read, so the WHO statement is known only through this table.
